summary: Technical deep dive focused on throughput tuning: continuous batching behavior, scheduler knobs, max_num_seqs, token limits, KV cache interactions, and quantization tradeoffs for a VPC/on-prem pilot. Agreed to run a short benchmark and iterate on scheduler settings; Redwood to supply runbook and recommended parameters.
transcript: 00:00 Jamie Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Jamie from Redwood, AE for NexaHealth. We'll run through throughput tuning and then leave time for q's. Arjun, want to intro?

00:12 Arjun Patel: Sure, Arjun here, staff SE on the inference runtime team — we'll focus on continuous batching, scheduler knobs like max_num_seqs and token limits, and how k v cache and quantization interact with throughput.
00:22 Laura Chen: Thanks. Our main goal is to get predictably low p95 latency at peak and keep token cost reasonable, we run mixed workloads, some long documents, some short chat.
00:35 Miguel Santos: Also important for us: VPC-only deployment and no outbound egress except to specific endpoints. We'll likely do Private deployment, maybe on-prem.

00:47 Jamie Park: Got it. We'll cover VPC considerations at the end. First, high level: continuous batching tries to fill batches dynamically based on inflight requests and latency SLOs. That trades a little latency for much higher throughput.

01:05 Arjun Patel: Right — our scheduler has a few knobs. max_num_seqs controls how many concurrent sequences we run in a single batch. There's also max_tokens_per_batch and a latency cap parameter. In practice you tune max_num_seqs up until GPU utilization tops out or latency SLOs are hit.
01:27 Ravi Kumar: When you say sequences, is that user sessions or inference requests? We have lots of short prompts — 8-12 tokens average.

01:34 Arjun Patel: It's per in-flight request sequence. Short prompts actually help batching because you can fit many sequences per batch. For chat-like short messages you can push max_num_seqs higher. For long-document generation we limit by token budget.
01:50 Miguel Santos: Any default values you recommend?

01:54 Arjun Patel: Defaults depend on model size and GPU. For a 70B int8 model on A100s we often start with max_num_seqs=32 and max_tokens_per_batch=4096, but for smaller models you can go higher. We'll send a table.
02:10 Laura Chen: Can you explain how KV cache affects batching and memory pressure? We do a lot of multi-turn chat where KV cache grows.

02:20 Arjun Patel: Sure — KV cache scales with sequence length; if your prompt + history is long, each sequence uses more KV memory. So the effective batch size (in terms of memory) is sum(seq_len) across sequences. Our scheduler uses an effective token budget to avoid OOMs. If you have big histories, reduce max_num_seqs or enable prefix/KV caching eviction policies.
02:44 Jamie Park: Quick note — sometimes the transcription and docs call it 'k v' cache or 'kv cache' — internal docs might show it as k v. So if you see odd spacing don't worry.
02:52 Miguel Santos: OK. About quantization — we want to use 4-bit quant for cost but worried about latency regressions. Any tradeoffs?

03:01 Arjun Patel: Quantization reduces memory and can increase throughput, but certain kernels and attention optimizations are different. For some model families, int4 gives slightly higher token generation latency per token but enables much larger batch sizes. Often a net win for throughput and cost. We recommend testing in your workload because accuracy regressions also matter.
03:23 Laura Chen: If int4 slightly slows per-token latency but allows double the batch size, p95 at peak might still be better, right?
03:30 Arjun Patel: Exactly — that's the common tradeoff. The scheduler can prefer higher batching when you accept slightly higher tail latency up to a configured SLO.
03:40 Ravi Kumar: How do you set the latency cap parameter? We have a 300ms p95 SLO for interactive experiences.

03:47 Arjun Patel: You set latency_cap_ms, e.g., 200-250ms to leave headroom. The scheduler uses that cap to wait for additional sequences up to that time window. If requests don't accumulate quickly, it will flush early. Important to align cap with real request arrival patterns. We'll share a graph that shows throughput vs latency cap.

04:10 Jamie Park: Also note token limits: there's per-request token_limit and per-batch token budget. If you have unpredictable long generations, we recommend per-request caps to prevent one request from starving the batch.
04:24 Miguel Santos: Do you recommend adaptive token caps that adjust live?

04:29 Arjun Patel: We have an adaptive scheduler prototype that reduces max_num_seqs for sequences that exceed median length, but for most customers static caps with periodic tuning are simpler. Adaptive is something we can pilot.
04:44 Laura Chen: About measuring: what logs or metrics should we collect during our 1-hour benchmark?

04:50 Jamie Park: Capture per-token latency, batch sizes distribution, GPU utilization, OOMs, KV cache size per step, and tracer spans for scheduling waits. We'll provide an agent script that emits these to the shared bucket.
05:05 Miguel Santos: Please add network egress and VPC flow logs — we need to audit traffic during pilot.
05:10 Jamie Park: Absolutely, we'll include the VPC checklist.

05:15 Arjun Patel: One subtlety: in VPC/on-prem we sometimes see higher variance in arrival patterns because of client-side batching and retries; that affects the scheduler. So we suggest running with synthetic traces that mimic production arrival patterns, including burstiness.
05:33 Laura Chen: For our mixed workload, what's a good starting profile? 70% short chat, 20% medium, 10% long?

05:40 Arjun Patel: That seems reasonable. For short chat, set max_num_seqs higher (32-64 depending on GPU), for medium reduce to 16-32, and for long reduce to 4-8 and rely on token limits. The scheduler can use route-specific configs per model endpoint.
06:00 Ravi Kumar: Any specific kernel quirks for our requested model family, Llama-3-ish? We saw some aks kernel mismatch earlier.

06:07 Arjun Patel: For certain Llama variants, fused attention kernels are preferred; if a particular kernel isn't available on your hardware, the runtime falls back to a slower path. We'll validate kernel matrix with your instance types. Please share exact image and CUDA versions.
06:22 Miguel Santos: We run RHEL8 with CUDA 12 and A100s. I'll put exact AMI and driver versions in the shared note.

06:30 Jamie Park: Great. Another thing: warm vs cold KV cache. For many chat use cases, warm cache (prefix caching) speeds up subsequent responses. If you want low-latency single-shot responses, prefetching strategies can be used. We'll include prewarm guidance.
06:46 Laura Chen: How does prewarming interact with batching? If prewarming consumes KV memory, does it reduce effective batch size?

06:53 Arjun Patel: Yes — prewarmed KV takes memory. The scheduler accounts for large prefixes as increased token cost per sequence, so your batch size will be reduced accordingly. There's a knob for 'prefix_cache_priority' that lets you trade off prewarm usage vs batch size. We'll include examples.
07:12 Miguel Santos: Is there tooling to simulate prefix-heavy traffic?
07:16 Arjun Patel: Yup — the benchmark script has modes to replay traces with long prefixes. We'll include a sample trace from an enterprise customer (anonymized).
07:25 Jamie Park: Quick interruption — there's a question in chat from Ravi: "When should we prefer Dedicated reserved capacity vs hosted for throughput tuning?"
07:33 Ravi Kumar (chat): prefer dedicated if predictable throughput and isolation required, right?

07:36 Jamie Park: Right — Dedicated gives more predictable GPU availability which is useful for consistent throughput. Hosted can be lower friction but you might see occasional fallbacks to smaller variants if capacity is constrained. For on-prem Private deployments, you'll have full control over schedulers and kernel builds.
07:55 Laura Chen: Any gotchas with autoscaling and continuous batching? We've seen autoscalers downscale too quickly during bursts.

08:02 Arjun Patel: Autoscaling needs a cool-down policy and should consider queue depth, not just CPU. We recommend a scale-up based on queue length and scale-down with a longer grace period. Also prefer burst pools if you have predictable spikes.
08:16 Miguel Santos: You mentioned 'burst pools' — is that in Dedicated only?
08:20 Jamie Park: Currently burst pools are supported in Dedicated and Hosted with reserved burst credits; on-prem can emulate via spare capacity. We'll send the dedicated burst documentation link.
08:30 Ravi Kumar: How do retries and client-side timeouts affect batching? We use aggressive client retries.

08:36 Arjun Patel: Retries can cause thundering herd effects and pollute the batching queue. Use idempotency keys and exponential backoff on the client side. The runtime also deduplicates identical requests within a short window in some cases.
08:50 Laura Chen: Ok thanks. Let's talk about concrete tuning plan for the pilot — what parameters should we try first?

08:56 Arjun Patel: Start with three configs: conservative, balanced, aggressive. Conservative: max_num_seqs=8, max_tokens_per_batch=2048, latency_cap_ms=120. Balanced: max_num_seqs=16-32, max_tokens_per_batch=4096, latency_cap_ms=200. Aggressive: max_num_seqs=48-64, max_tokens_per_batch=8192, latency_cap_ms=300. We'll tailor numbers to your GPU.
09:20 Miguel Santos: Those look good. How long should each run be?
09:24 Arjun Patel: 1 hour per config is often enough to see steady-state, but run longer if you have diurnal patterns. We'll recommend 60-90 minutes per config.
09:33 Jamie Park: We'll also provide an evaluation deck that maps results to cost and latency tradeoffs. Expect a CSV with per-second batch sizes, p50/p95/p99 latencies, GPU util, and cost estimate.
09:46 Laura Chen: Can Redwood help with running the benchmark in our VPC? We prefer you provide the scripts and we run them internally.

09:52 Jamie Park: Yes, we'll provide scripts and a quickstart. For security we're happy to do a runbook walkthrough via screenshare and you run the jobs in your environment. We'll also provide a parsing notebook to visualize results.
10:05 Ravi Kumar: On quantization evaluation — do you provide automated evals for quality regressions? We need to ensure no more than 0.5% drop in accuracy on our NER tasks.

10:13 Arjun Patel: We have an eval harness that runs against your prompt sets. For quantization, we recommend running the evals pre/post and using Redwood Optimize recommendations. We'll include the eval harness instructions.
10:28 Miguel Santos: One last infra question: OOMs during batching — what's typical root cause?

10:33 Arjun Patel: Usually either misconfigured max_tokens_per_batch or unexpectedly long prefixes causing KV growth. Also certain fused kernels require extra workspace. The runtime logs out-of-memory with a stack trace; we'll help interpret. The benchmark script captures those OOM events.
10:48 Laura Chen: Great. Can you summarize the immediate deliverables?

10:52 Jamie Park: Sure — deliverables: 1) throughput tuning runbook and scheduler knobs doc, 2) recommended conservative/balanced/aggressive configs for your GPU, 3) benchmark scripts + sample traces, 4) VPC/on-prem checklist and security docs, 5) eval harness for quantization checks. We'll send these after the call.
11:14 Ravi Kumar: Sounds good. Let's schedule the follow-up after we run the three configs. Week of 2026-04-06 works for us.
11:21 Jamie Park: I'll set a calendar invite; Arjun will join for analysis. Anything else?
11:26 Laura Chen: Please include an example of max_num_seqs vs batch size chart in the doc — very helpful.
11:31 Arjun Patel: Will do. Also linking to a kernel-matrix checklist; Miguel please share exact CUDA/driver details.
11:40 Miguel Santos: I'll add them to the shared drive. Thanks everyone.
11:44 Jamie Park: Thanks all, we'll follow up with the artifacts. Meeting adjourned.
